title: Low-Level Errors Leaking Through Domain Interfaces
pattern: A high-level domain or business interface exposes driver-, system-, or infrastructure-specific errors (like `sqlx::Error` or `std::io::Error`) in its signature rather than errors appropriate to its abstraction level, whether as a `Result` error type or as a declared exception specification.
why_bad: It breaks encapsulation. Callers become tightly coupled to the underlying database library or I/O engine, so changing a driver or its error vocabulary forces signature and handling changes through every intermediate layer up the stack, preventing modularity and refactoring [28:431].
detection: Inspect domain methods and business functions for concrete database, filesystem, or other low-level implementation error types in (a) their `Result`/return error types, or (b) their exception-propagation declarations (`throws`/`throw(...)` clauses). Confirm that the error crosses an intended abstraction boundary rather than belonging to a single-layer utility API.
fix: Catch the low-level failure at the boundary and translate or wrap it into an accurate domain-level error category that matches the abstraction level of the calling module, preserving the diagnostic cause where appropriate [28:432]. Distinguish missing data from unavailability, timeout, or other failures instead of mapping every error to a not-found result.
source: *Code Complete* (McConnell), Chapter 8 [28:431]; Robert C. Martin, *Clean Code*, Chapter 7.
